Title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in agentic systems that interact with untrusted environments. However, LLM agents are vulnerable to prompt injection attacks when handling untrusted data. In this paper, we propose Ca Me L, a robust defense that creates a protective system layer around the LLM, securing it even when underlying models are susceptible to attacks. To operate, Ca Me L explicitly extracts the control and data flows from the (trusted) user query; therefore, untrusted data retrieved by the LLM can never affect the program flow. Moreover, to prevent the exfiltration of private data over unauthorized data flows, Ca Me L enforces security policies over assigned flow tags for each tool call. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Ca Me L by solving 77% of tasks in Agent Dojo with security guarantees (compared to 84% with an undefended system). We release the code for Ca Me L at https://github.com/google-research/camel-prompt-injection.
Major_Contribution_Result: CaMeL is a system-layer defense that extracts control and data flows from the trusted user query, executes via a custom interpreter tracking provenance, and enforces capability/security policies so untrusted data cannot alter control flow or unauthorized data flows. On AgentDojo it solves 77% of tasks with security guarantees versus 84% for an undefended system. Code is released publicly.
Research_Limitations_Challenges: Authors state CaMeL does not defend text-to-text attacks without control/data-flow consequences (e.g., misleading summaries or phishing links without private-data exfiltration). It is not fully autonomous—users may need to clarify ambiguous flows. They discuss capability-system adoption costs, ecosystem participation needs, side-channels (including exception-based issues mitigated partly by STRICT mode), and that the design does not cover every attack vector.
Critics: One of the more system-security-principled agent defenses evaluated on AgentDojo with an explicit utility trade-off (77% vs 84%). Guarantees are relative to enforced control/data-flow policies, not to all semantic manipulations. Comparison to other defenses should respect that out-of-scope attacks are acknowledged by the authors.
